analogy.p: Imagine a workshop with **one bookshelf** (memory) that holds both the **recipe books** (instructions) and the **ingredients** (data), and a **single corridor** (the bus) to it. One assistant (the CPU) walks down the corridor, brings back one thing at a time, then uses it. Because there is only one shelf and one corridor, the assistant cannot carry a recipe and an ingredient together; that wait is the **bottleneck**. The analogy breaks down because a real computer fetches in binary at huge speeds, and real CPUs have caches that act like a small table close to the assistant to cut down trips.
analogy.t: A single library shelf and one assistant

bullets: Know that Von Neumann architecture uses **one memory** for **both instructions and data**.
Know this is the **stored program concept**: programs are loaded into memory, then executed by the CPU.
Know the roles of **PC, MAR, MDR and ACC**.
Know the CPU parts used: **CU, ALU, registers, cache**.
Know the three buses: **address, data, control** (commonly taught alongside it).
Describe how the **fetch-decode-execute cycle** uses the registers.
Know a limitation: the **Von Neumann bottleneck**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 1.1 requires you to know the **purpose and function of the Von Neumann architecture**: the design used by most general-purpose computers in which **both program instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory** and are processed by a CPU using the fetch-decode-execute cycle. You must be able to name the key components and registers it uses (**CPU, memory, input/output, PC, MAR, MDR, ACC**) and describe how they work together. Questions often ask you to describe the architecture, state what a register does, or explain the idea of a stored program.

bullets: **Instructions and data are both stored as binary** in the same memory.
The CPU **cannot tell by looking at a binary pattern** whether it is an instruction or data; it depends on how and when it is fetched.
A program is **loaded from secondary storage into RAM** before it can be run.
The CPU **fetches instructions one at a time in sequence** (unless a branch or jump changes the order).
Changing the program only needs **different contents in memory**, not a hardware change.
The architecture is named after **John von Neumann**, a mathematician who described the model.
Almost all PCs, laptops and phones are based on this idea.
core.p: Before stored-program computers, machines were rewired or reconfigured by hand for each new task. John von Neumann described a design (1945) in which the **instructions of a program are stored in memory in binary, exactly like data**. The computer can then load any program into memory and run it simply by fetching its instructions one at a time. This makes computers **general purpose and programmable**: the same hardware can run a game, a word processor or a calculator just by loading different instructions into memory.

bullets: **CPU**: processes instructions using the CU, ALU and registers.
**Main memory (RAM)**: stores the program instructions and the data they use, in binary, at numbered **addresses**.
**Input/Output**: devices such as keyboard, mouse, screen and storage that feed data in and out.
**Control unit**: fetches, decodes and controls execution.
**ALU**: arithmetic and logic.
**Buses**: address bus, data bus and control bus connect the CPU to memory and I/O.
Secondary storage holds programs until they are **loaded into RAM**.
core.h: The main components of the architecture
core.p: A Von Neumann computer has a **CPU** (containing the control unit, ALU and registers), **main memory (RAM)** holding both instructions and data, and **input/output (I/O)** devices for communication with the outside world. These parts are linked by **buses**: groups of wires that carry signals. The CPU does the processing, the memory stores what is being processed, and the I/O connects the user and other devices.

bullets: **Address bus**: one-directional, **CPU to memory**; its width decides how many locations can be addressed.
**Data bus**: **bidirectional**; width decides how many bits can be transferred at once.
**Control bus**: carries signals such as **memory read, memory write** and clock.
An **n-bit address bus** can address **2^n** locations: 16 bits gives 65 536 locations; 32 bits gives 4 294 967 296.
A wider data bus moves more bits per transfer, so can improve speed.
All instructions and data share **the same bus system** in Von Neumann machines.
Because buses are shared, only **one transfer** can take place at a time.
core.p: A **bus** is a set of parallel wires used to send binary signals between components. The **address bus** carries the **address** of the memory location the CPU wants to access; it is **one-way** (from the CPU to memory). The **data bus** carries the actual **data or instructions** and is **two-way**, because data goes both from memory to the CPU (read) and from CPU to memory (write). The **control bus** carries **control signals** such as read, write and clock signals, to coordinate the components.

bullets: **PC**: stores the **address of the next instruction**; incremented each fetch.
**MAR**: stores the **address** of the location to read or write; connects to the **address bus**.
**MDR**: stores the **content** (data or instruction) read from or to be written to memory; connects to the **data bus**.
**ACC**: stores the **results of calculations** from the ALU.
Registers are **volatile** and very small.
Only one instruction is held in the pipeline of this simple model at a time.
Do not confuse **MAR (address)** with **MDR (data)**.
core.h: The registers used in the architecture
core.p: The Von Neumann model uses four named registers. The **Program Counter (PC)** holds the address of the next instruction. The **Memory Address Register (MAR)** holds the address of the memory location being accessed. The **Memory Data Register (MDR)** holds the data or instruction just read from memory or about to be written. The **Accumulator (ACC)** holds the result of ALU operations. They are inside the CPU so that the CPU can work with values much faster than RAM allows.

bullets: Step 1: **PC to MAR** (the address of the instruction is copied).
Step 2: address goes along the **address bus**; **read signal** on the control bus.
Step 3: the instruction goes from memory **along the data bus to the MDR**.
Step 4: **PC is incremented** to the next address.
The instruction in the MDR is then passed to the **control unit** for decoding.
Fetching an instruction uses the **same bus and memory** as fetching data.
Mark scheme words: 'copied', 'address bus', 'MAR', 'MDR', 'incremented'.
core.h: The fetch stage using the registers
core.p: During **fetch**, the CPU gets the next instruction from memory. The **address in the PC is copied to the MAR**. The address is sent along the **address bus** to memory, and the control unit sends a **read signal** along the control bus. The instruction stored at that address is sent back along the **data bus** into the **MDR**. Finally the **PC is incremented** by 1 so it points to the next instruction (this may be changed later by a jump or branch instruction).

bullets: **Decode**: CU works out the **opcode and operand**.
**Execute (calculation)**: **ALU** operates; **result stored in ACC**.
**Execute (load)**: operand address to **MAR**, data from memory into **MDR**, then to **ACC**.
**Execute (store)**: ACC value to **MDR**, address in **MAR**, written to memory.
**Execute (branch/jump)**: the **PC is overwritten** with a new address.
After execute the **cycle repeats** with the next instruction.
The cycle runs continuously, billions of times per second, controlled by the **clock**.
core.h: Decode and execute using the registers
core.p: In **decode**, the control unit examines the instruction in the MDR (passed on to the instruction decoder) and splits it into an **opcode** (what to do) and an **operand** (the data or address involved). In **execute**, the CU sends control signals so the instruction is carried out: an arithmetic or logic operation is done by the **ALU** and the result goes into the **ACC**; a load instruction copies a value from memory through the MAR and MDR into the ACC; a store instruction writes the ACC value back to memory via the MDR and MAR.

bullets: Start: **PC = 0**, ACC = 0.
Fetch 1: MAR = 0, MDR = LOAD 10, PC becomes **1**.
Execute 1: MAR = 10, MDR = 5, **ACC = 5**.
Fetch 2: MAR = 1, MDR = ADD 11, PC becomes **2**.
Execute 2: MAR = 11, MDR = 3, ALU computes 5 + 3, **ACC = 8**.
Fetch 3: MAR = 2, MDR = STORE 12, PC becomes **3**; execute: MAR = 12, MDR = 8, **8 stored in address 12**.
Final: **PC = 3, ACC = 8**.
core.p: A trace table shows how the register contents change instruction by instruction. Suppose memory address 0 holds LOAD 10, address 1 holds ADD 11, address 2 holds STORE 12; address 10 holds the value 5 and address 11 holds the value 3. Starting with PC = 0, each instruction is fetched, decoded and executed in turn, changing the PC, MAR, MDR and ACC. You may be asked to complete a table like this or to say what is in a register at a certain point.

bullets: **One memory** for instructions and data: simpler design and lower cost.
Memory is **shared flexibly**: space can be used for programs or data as needed.
**Programs can be easily changed** or loaded: any program can run on the same hardware.
The control unit is **simpler** as it only has one path to manage.
Allows **operating systems** to load many different programs.
Programs can themselves be **treated as data** (for example by a compiler or a loader).
Used in virtually **all general-purpose computers**.
core.h: Advantages of the Von Neumann architecture
core.p: The key strengths of Von Neumann design are its **simplicity and flexibility**. Because one memory and one set of buses store and carry everything, the control logic is simpler and **cheaper to build**. The programmer or operating system can decide how much memory to give to instructions and how much to data, and programs can be **loaded, replaced and updated** easily. This flexibility is why general-purpose computers use it.

bullets: **Only one memory access at a time** over the shared bus.
The CPU can **wait** for memory, wasting cycles.
Instructions are processed **sequentially** in the simple model.
A faulty program could **overwrite instructions** held in the same memory.
**Cache** reduces the bottleneck by keeping data near the CPU.
**Harvard architecture** (not required by OCR) uses separate memories and buses for instructions and data.
Mention of the bottleneck is usually **a 1 or 2 mark** extension answer.
core.p: Because instructions and data share the **same memory and same bus**, the CPU cannot fetch an instruction and read data at the same moment; it must do them one after the other. The CPU is also much faster than memory, so it often waits. This limit on throughput between CPU and memory is called the **Von Neumann bottleneck**. Cache and multiple cores reduce the problem but do not remove it, and an instruction can in principle accidentally **overwrite** program data if the program is faulty.

bullets: Von Neumann: **one memory, one set of buses**; Harvard: **two memories, two sets of buses**.
Harvard can **fetch instruction and data at once**.
Von Neumann is **simpler and cheaper**; Harvard needs more wiring.
Von Neumann is **more flexible** about memory use.
Modern CPUs mix both: **separate L1 caches** for instructions and data but **one main RAM**.
Embedded devices (microcontrollers) often use Harvard.
Only **Von Neumann** is in the J277 specification.
core.p: Harvard architecture stores instructions and data in **separate memories with separate buses**, so an instruction fetch and a data access can happen at the same time. It is common in some **embedded systems and signal processors**, where speed and predictability matter. Von Neumann machines trade a little speed for simplicity and flexibility. OCR J277 does not require Harvard architecture, but knowing the contrast helps you understand why the shared memory of Von Neumann is both its strength and its weakness.

bullets: Links to **cs.0.1 fetch-decode-execute cycle**.
Links to **cs.0.2 CPU components**.
Links to **cs.0.4 CPU performance**: cache reduces memory waits.
Links to **1.2 primary storage**: RAM holds the running program and data.
Links to **machine code** and **binary** in unit 1.2 and 2.x.
Links to **assembly language** used in J277 for low-level instructions (LMC style questions).
Links to **operating systems**: the OS loads programs into memory.
core.h: Von Neumann and the rest of the spec
core.p: The Von Neumann architecture links directly to nearly all of the 1.1 and 1.2 topics. The **fetch-decode-execute cycle** is its operating rhythm. **CPU components** (CU, ALU, cache, registers) are its processing parts. **RAM** is its main memory, and **secondary storage** supplies programs that are loaded into it. **Performance factors** (clock speed, cores, cache) are ways of getting more work through the CPU-memory bottleneck.

bullets: **2 marks**: instructions and data are stored together (1) in the same memory in binary (1).
Use words **'copied'** for PC to MAR and **'incremented'** for PC.
Avoid saying the **MAR holds data**: it holds an **address**.
For **trace tables**, update the PC at fetch and ACC at execute.
State the **limitation** if asked for drawbacks: bottleneck.
For '**explain why**' add a because: 'because instructions and data share a bus'.
Show **units and binary** neatly when addresses and values are involved.
core.p: Typical questions are 'State what is meant by Von Neumann architecture' (2 marks), 'Describe the purpose of the MAR' (1-2 marks), and 'Describe the fetch stage' (up to 4 marks). Use the precise wording 'stored program' and 'instructions **and** data in the same memory'. For the cycle, write the steps in the right order using register names and say whether they are copied, incremented or read.

exam: **State what is meant by the Von Neumann architecture [2 marks]**: instructions and data stored together (1) in the same memory/processed by a CPU using fetch-decode-execute (1).
**Describe the purpose of the MAR / MDR / PC / ACC [1 to 2 marks]**: use exact function wording, never swap address and data.
**Describe the fetch stage [3 to 4 marks]**: PC copied to MAR; address sent via address bus, read signal; instruction travels on data bus to MDR; PC incremented.
**Complete a trace table**: update PC at fetch, MAR/MDR when memory is accessed, ACC when a result is produced.
**Give one advantage and one disadvantage**: simpler/flexible vs bottleneck from shared bus/memory.
**Describe the stored program concept**: instructions in memory as binary like data; fetched and executed one at a time; allows any program to be loaded.
**Command word 'identify'** or 'state': one-line answers; 'explain': add because.
**Bus questions**: say the **direction** of the address bus (one way) and data bus (both ways).
**Address bus width**: number of addresses = 2 to the power of the number of bits.
Use **the register names the question uses**, and write full names at least once.

mistakes.r: Von Neumann architecture means **instructions and data are stored together in the same memory** (stored program), processed by the CPU.
mistakes.w: Von Neumann means the CPU has an ALU and a CU.

mistakes.r: The **MAR holds an address**; the **MDR holds the data/instruction**.
mistakes.w: The MAR holds the data from memory.

mistakes.r: The **PC holds the address of the next instruction**.
mistakes.w: The PC holds the instruction being executed.

mistakes.r: The PC address is **copied to the MAR**; the ALU does calculations, with results in the **ACC**.
mistakes.w: The PC goes straight to the ALU.

mistakes.r: The **address bus is one-way** (CPU to memory); the **data bus is two-way**.
In Von Neumann design **both are stored in the same memory (RAM)**.
mistakes.w: Instructions are stored in ROM and data in RAM, as in Von Neumann.

mistakes.r: The bottleneck is because **instructions and data share one bus and memory**, so only one can be accessed at a time and the CPU waits.
mistakes.w: The bottleneck is because the CPU is too slow.

mistakes.r: The PC is **incremented during the fetch stage**, ready for the next instruction (unless a jump changes it).
mistakes.w: The PC is incremented after execute.

summary: The spec asks you to know that the Von Neumann architecture stores instructions and data together in the same main memory (the stored program concept), and to describe how the CPU, memory, buses and the registers PC, MAR, MDR and ACC work together in the fetch-decode-execute cycle. It matters because it is the design of almost all modern computers and the basis of many exam questions on the CPU.

terms.d: A computer design in which program instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory and processed by a CPU.
The idea that instructions are stored in memory as binary, like data, and fetched and executed by the CPU one at a time.
Register holding the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
Register holding the address of the memory location to be read from or written to.
Register holding the data or instruction that has been read from, or is to be written to, memory.
Register that holds the result of calculations done by the ALU.
A set of parallel wires used to carry binary signals between components.
One-way bus carrying the address of the memory location from the CPU to memory.
Two-way bus carrying data and instructions between the CPU, memory and I/O.
Bus carrying control signals such as read, write and clock from the control unit.
The repeated process of fetching an instruction from memory, decoding it and executing it.
The part of an instruction that says what operation to carry out.
The part of an instruction that gives the data, or the address of the data, to operate on.
The limit on speed caused by instructions and data sharing one memory and bus, so the CPU must wait.
A design with separate memories and buses for instructions and data (not required by J277).
RAM: the primary storage in which the running program and its data are held.

worked.ans: PC copied to MAR; address sent via the address bus with a read signal; instruction travels along the data bus into the MDR; PC incremented.
worked.q: Describe the fetch stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle using the Von Neumann registers. [4 marks]
steps: The address in the PC is copied to the MAR (1).
The address is sent on the address bus and the control unit sends a read signal (1).
The instruction is sent from memory along the data bus to the MDR (1).
The PC is incremented to point to the next instruction (1).

worked.q: A program is stored in memory: address 0 = LOAD 10, address 1 = ADD 11, address 2 = STORE 12. Address 10 holds 5 and address 11 holds 3. Give the values of the PC and ACC after the three instructions are complete and state what is stored at address 12. [3 marks]
steps: Each fetch increments the PC: 0 to 1 to 2 to 3, so PC = 3 (1).
STORE 12 copies the ACC value to memory so address 12 holds 8 (1).

worked.ans: Instructions and data share one memory and bus, so the CPU can only do one access at a time (the Von Neumann bottleneck) and must wait, which slows processing.
worked.q: State two limitations of the Von Neumann architecture and explain one. [3 marks]
steps: Limitation 1: the Von Neumann bottleneck: instructions and data share the same bus (1).
Limitation 2: only one memory access can take place at a time, so the CPU waits (1).
Explain: because they share a bus the CPU cannot fetch an instruction and data together, so it spends time waiting and processing is slower (1).
